name: Surfwear

lead: Surfwear is clothing rooted in surf culture: boardshorts, rash guards, graphic tees, hoodies and loose casual pieces. Worn by non-surfers, it signals a laid-back, outdoorsy style.
Brands such as Quiksilver, Billabong and Rip Curl turned surf apparel into a global fashion category in the 1980s and 1990s, according to Grokipedia.

paras: People wear it as everyday casualwear: boardshorts or relaxed shorts, logo tees and hoodies in washed or colourful graphics, often with sandals or sneakers.
No health risks; relaxed fits do not flatter every build, and fashion fit preferences vary.

angle.text: Surfwear gives a casual outfit language built on loose shorts, graphic tees and hoodies that conveys an easy-going, coastal image.

lead: Surfwear is casual clothing inspired by surf culture, covering both performance garments (boardshorts, rash guards) and lifestyle pieces worn by non-surfers. As a style it offers a relaxed, beach-oriented look.[1]

Boardshorts were part of 1960s Southern California surf culture, and many surf brands began as cottage industries supplying local surfers.[2] Grokipedia traces the category from Hawaiian and early Californian beach attire to Australian brands Rip Curl (1969), Quiksilver and Billabong (1973), which grew into mainstream fashion in the 1980s and 1990s.[1] Since the 2010s sustainability has become prominent, with brands using recycled fabrics.[1]
infobox: Quiksilver, Billabong, Rip Curl, Hurley, Stussy

paras: Designs commonly feature colourful graphics, logos and ocean motifs; functional items offer durability, UV protection and resistance to saltwater.[1]

Early surfers in Hawaii wore minimal attire, then woollen tank suits, then shorter trunks in the 1930s; Californian surfers improvised cut-off pants in the 1940s.[1] Boardshorts appeared as 1960s California baggies.[2] Quick-drying nylon replaced cotton in later decades.[1]

timeline.event: Rip Curl founded in Torquay, Australia.[1]
Association of Surfing Professionals established, increasing surf media exposure.[1]
